synopsis: False alarms and unnecessary interventions should be measured against representative operational exposure, such as operating hours, loading cycles or close approaches, rather than staged tests or discovery-campaign failure fractions [f11336, f3342, f134]. No published authoritative off-road acceptance rates were found, so programs must set their own criteria separately for advisory warnings, urgent warnings, speed reduction and full braking, with nuisance-stop thresholds agreed with site operations [f2121, f2880, f2124, f10716]. Under a homogeneous Poisson model, zero events in T hours gives a one-sided 95% upper rate bound of approximately 3/T: 300 representative event-free hours supports fewer than one unnecessary brake per 100 hours, and 3,000 supports fewer than one per 1,000 hours; clustered alarms require different statistical models [f5456, f6658, f6659, f6660]. Shadow-mode logging and replay can estimate unnecessary braking per operating hour by site type and weather, while field testing should use continuous, untriggered recording in representative site classes [f1601, f5472]. Accident counts cannot establish comparable collision rates without exposure denominators and compatible categories, and even ten million operating hours with few recorded incidents says little about detector performance without encounter counts and recording completeness [f11610, f3047, f7939].

Both require program-level acceptance criteria; Chapter 3 distinguishes intervention levels.
